title: Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation: An Attentional Integration
key_findings: Automation complacency appears under multiple-task load, in naive and expert users, and is not removed by simple practice (up to 60 min of training did not reduce it, Singh, Sharma & Parasuraman 2001).
Constant-reliability automation: 33% of automation failures detected vs 82% under variable reliability (Parasuraman, Molloy & Singh 1993); single-task detection ~97%.
Automation bias produces omission and commission errors; not prevented by training or instructions to verify; affects individuals and teams.

Mosier et al. 1992: 75% of pilots followed a wrong automated-checklist recommendation vs 25% with a paper checklist; Mosier et al. 1998: 100% shut down an engine on a false EICAS alert and 67% reported a 'phantom memory' of confirming cues.

Felt accountability reduces automation bias (Skitka, Mosier & Burdick 2000); experiencing automation failures during training reduces commission errors (Bahner, Huper & Manzey 2008); 20-50% commission errors at the first wrong diagnosis.
Aids that give information/status show less automation bias than aids that give specific commands; trial-by-trial confidence information reduced decrements (McGuirl & Sarter 2006).
practical_applications: Design human checkpoints so the human must look at the raw output, not only at a green tick.
Seed review batches with known-bad items so reviewers meet automation failures early.
Show the check's evidence (status) rather than only a verdict (command).
limitations: Mostly aviation, medicine and process-control lab studies; transfer to creative media is an inference.
Some effects (first-failure effect, command vs status) did not replicate consistently.

title: Ironies of automation
key_findings: The designer who tries to eliminate the operator still leaves the operator the tasks the designer cannot think how to automate - an arbitrary collection with little support.

Vigilance: humans cannot keep effective visual attention on a source where little happens for more than about half an hour; rare abnormalities must be caught by alarms, which raises the question of who notices when the alarm system is not working.
Automatic control can 'camouflage' failure until trends are beyond control; 'automatic systems should fail obviously'.
Manual skills deteriorate when not used; takeover needs a more, not less, skilled operator.
'Perhaps the final irony is that it is the most successful automated systems, with rare need for manual intervention, which may need the greatest investment in human operator training.'
The human must know which tasks the computer is dealing with and how.
practical_applications: Make pipeline steps fail loudly (non-zero exit, stop the batch) instead of silently producing a plausible file.
Keep the human doing some manual picks so the skill of judging seeds stays sharp.
Log what each automated step did so the human knows what the machine handled.
limitations: Process-control context (1983); argument paper, not an experiment.
license: copyrighted (Elsevier); free copy hosted by third party

title: Humans and Automation: Use, Misuse, Disuse, Abuse
key_findings: Misuse = over-reliance (monitoring failures, decision biases); disuse = neglect, commonly caused by false alarms when base rates are ignored; abuse = automating functions without regard for consequences to human performance.
Monitoring of automation is affected by workload, automation reliability and consistency, and the saliency of automation state indicators.
practical_applications: Tune automated checks for false-alarm rate, or people stop reading them (disuse).
Do not automate a step just because it can be automated (abuse).
limitations: Read as abstract only.

title: A model for types and levels of human interaction with automation
authors: Raja Parasuraman; Thomas B. Sheridan; Christopher D. Wickens
key_findings: Automation can apply to four function classes - information acquisition, information analysis, decision/action selection, action implementation - each on a continuum from manual to fully automatic.

Automation does not merely supplant but changes human activity and imposes new coordination demands; primary evaluative criterion = human performance consequences; secondary = automation reliability and cost of decision/action consequences.
practical_applications: Map each pipeline step to the four classes and choose a level per step (auto-generate, human-select, auto-finish, human-publish).
limitations: Model paper; read as abstract only.

title: Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance
authors: John D. Lee; Katrina A. See
key_findings: People fail to rely on automation appropriately; trust guides reliance when complexity makes a complete understanding impractical.
Conceptual model of trust dynamics, context and display characteristics; the goal is appropriate (calibrated) reliance, not maximal trust.
practical_applications: Show per-run evidence (contact sheet, metrics) so trust in a script tracks its real reliability.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Ironies of Automation: Still Unresolved After All These Years
key_findings: Bainbridge's ironies remain relevant, are recognisable in later automation-related accidents, and still inspire researchers, accident investigators, regulators and managers.
practical_applications: Treat the ironies as current, not historical.
limitations: Abstract only; accident-focused.

title: Automation bias: a systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators
authors: Kate Goddard; Abdul Roudsari; Jeremy C. Wyatt
key_findings: 74 of 13,821 retrieved papers included; automation bias mediated by cognitive style, task-specific experience, trust and confidence; environmental mediators are workload, task complexity and time constraint.
Mitigators: training, emphasising user accountability, position of advice on screen, updated confidence levels, providing information rather than recommendation.
practical_applications: Review gates under time pressure (end of a long batch, late at night) are the most bias-prone; schedule review when not rushed.
limitations: Healthcare focus; abstract only.

title: Toyota Production System (Toyota global website)
key_findings: Jidoka = 'automation with a human touch': the line stops immediately when abnormalities are detected to prevent defective products; traced to Sakichi Toyoda's automatic loom which 'built the capability to make judgments into the machine itself'.
Andon signals abnormality so 'people need only respond when there is an abnormality'; Just-in-Time = make only what is needed, when it is needed, in the amount needed.
practical_applications: Stop the batch at the first abnormal output instead of finishing 100 bad images.
Generate only the sets that will be scheduled soon (JIT) rather than a large unscheduled backlog.
limitations: Corporate self-description.

title: Poka yoke (Lean Lexicon entry)
key_findings: Poka-yoke = simple, inexpensive error-proofing devices; purpose is 100% quality by finding defects at their source.

Shutdown devices (strongest: the machine will not start if the workpiece is set wrong) vs warning devices (buzzer/light); contrasted with sampling inspection (can miss defects) and 100% inspection (costly, after the fact).
practical_applications: Scripts refuse to run with wrong inputs (shutdown) or print loud warnings (warning).
limitations: The page does not name Shingo; attribution to Shigeo Shingo comes from secondary sources (search summary).

title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.1 How did Statistical Quality Control begin?
key_findings: Shewhart memo of 16 May 1924 with a sketch of a modern control chart; 1931 book Economic Control of Quality of Manufactured Product; Dodge and Romig (Bell Labs) led sampling inspection.
practical_applications: History anchor for control charts and sampling.
limitations: Brief history page.

title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook, 6.2.1 What is acceptance sampling?
key_findings: Acceptance sampling inspects a random sample of a lot and accepts or rejects the lot; its purpose is to decide acceptability, not to estimate quality.
Used when testing is destructive, or 100% inspection is very costly or too slow; plans are 'one-shot deals' for short-run effects; long-run quality needs control charts.
practical_applications: When a batch is too large to check every frame, sample randomly and redo the batch on a defect.
limitations: AQL tables not reproduced here.

title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook, 6.3.2 What are Variables Control Charts?
key_findings: 3-sigma control limits are the accepted industry standard; control limits are not specification limits.
Western Electric run rules (e.g., 8 consecutive points on one side of the centre line) flag non-random patterns; adding them raises false alarms from about 1 per 371 points to about 1 per 91.75.
practical_applications: Track reject rate per batch (FLUX seeds rejected per set) and look for runs, not single bad days.
limitations: Assumes roughly normal, independent data; small-count reject rates need p-charts.

title: Economic Control of Quality of Manufactured Product
key_findings: Founding text of statistical process control (as described by NIST).
practical_applications: Common vs special cause framing.
limitations: Not read; existence and role per NIST.

title: The Making of Toy Story
authors: Mark Henne; Hal Hickel; Ewan Johnson; Sonoko Konishi
doi_isbn: Proceedings of COMPCON Spring '96 (41st IEEE International Computer Conference), pp. 463-468
key_findings: Animated film creation is so sequential that efficient management of the pipeline is crucial; more than 1,500 shots kept logically consistent with sets and a shot database.
Ringmaster: relational database with inventories of models, textures and images; routes rendering requests to available machines on the RenderFarm, keeps status, then invokes compositing of layers.
RenderFarm of over 300 Sun processors plus SGI machines; idle personal workstations drawn into the batch pool; ~260 GB DiskFarm with ~140,000 image files.
practical_applications: A production database (asset inventory + job status) is the core of a pipeline, not the renderer.
Use idle machine time for batch jobs (overnight FLUX).
limitations: Practitioner conference paper; figures as reported by Pixar staff in 1996.

title: Introduction to USD (OpenUSD documentation)
key_findings: USD is roughly the fourth generation of composed scene description at Pixar (after Marionette, Presto, TidScene), initiated 2012.

Artists work in separate layers combined in a strength order, so each can work without overwriting others; stronger layers override weaker ones non-destructively; referencing assembles reusable assets.
practical_applications: Separate files per responsibility (story text, prompts, picks, finish settings) so parallel work does not overwrite.
limitations: Vendor documentation.

title: VFX Reference Platform
key_findings: Yearly set of target tool and library versions (compiler, Python, Qt, OpenEXR, OpenVDB) to minimise incompatibilities between software packages; CY2027 platform feature complete per 1 Nov 2026 update.
practical_applications: Pin one set of tool versions per season (Python, ComfyUI, model files) and change them on purpose.
limitations: Start year not stated on the page.

title: Make - a program for maintaining computer programs
key_findings: Make keeps track of relationships between parts of a program and issues the commands needed to make the parts consistent after changes; in use on UNIX since 1975; the idea adapts to many environments.
practical_applications: Dependency-aware 'skip if up to date' steps (gen.sh skips existing images) descend from make.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Continuous Integration
key_findings: Practices: single source repository, automate the build, self-testing build, everyone commits to mainline daily, fix broken builds immediately, keep the build fast (~10 min). First published 10 Sep 2000, revised 18 Jan 2024.
practical_applications: One command builds a kit end to end; a red check stops everything until fixed.
limitations: Software practice; evidence is experiential.

title: DORA's software delivery metrics (guide)
key_findings: Five metrics: change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time (throughput); change fail rate, deployment rework rate (instability).
'DORA's research has repeatedly demonstrated that speed and stability are not tradeoffs.'
practical_applications: Studio analogues: brief-to-publish lead time, redo rate after publish, time to fix a bad post.
limitations: Survey-based research programme; causal reading contested (not examined here).

title: Definitions (Reproducible Builds project)
key_findings: A build is reproducible if, given the same source code, build environment and build instructions, any party can recreate bit-by-bit identical copies of all specified artifacts; verified by hash comparison.
practical_applications: Record source (story file + commit), environment (model files, versions) and instructions (command line) per kit.
limitations: Bit-identical output is often impossible for GPU generative models; aim for 'same within tolerance'.

title: Reproducibility (Diffusers documentation, v0.43)
key_findings: Use a seeded Generator; a CPU generator is more stable across machines; a GPU generator can diverge from CPU results.
Deterministic algorithms (enable_full_determinism) may be slower; reproducibility 'is not guaranteed even with an identical seed'.
practical_applications: A seed is a recipe ingredient, not a guarantee; keep the accepted image itself.
limitations: Library-specific; ComfyUI behaviour may differ.

title: Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference
key_findings: Temperature-0 nondeterminism mainly comes from kernels lacking batch invariance (server load changes batch size), not simply concurrency plus floating point.
1,000 temperature-0 completions of one prompt gave 80 unique outputs; with batch-invariant kernels all 1,000 were identical; cost 26 s -> 42-55 s.
practical_applications: Do not expect a hosted LLM/TTS to return the same output twice; save the accepted output, not just the prompt.
limitations: Industry lab blog, not peer reviewed; one model/server stack.

title: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems
authors: D. Sculley; Gary Holt; Daniel Golovin; Eugene Davydov; Todd Phillips; et al.
key_findings: A mature ML system might be at most 5% ML code and at least 95% glue code.
Pipeline jungles: scrapes, joins and sampling steps with intermediate files; detecting errors and recovering from failures is difficult and costly; avoided only by holistic redesign.
Dead experimental codepaths accumulate; Knight Capital lost $465M in 45 minutes apparently due to obsolete experimental codepaths; configuration debt.
practical_applications: Per-day one-off tmp/*.py scripts (picks24, sigs25, finish26) are pipeline-jungle risk: promote stable ones into tools/ and delete dead ones.
limitations: Position paper from Google experience; not a controlled study.

title: Building effective agents
key_findings: Workflows = LLMs and tools orchestrated through predefined code paths; agents = the LLM dynamically directs its own process and tool use.
Patterns: prompt chaining with programmatic gates, routing, parallelization (sectioning/voting), orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer.
Start with the simplest solution and add complexity only when it measurably improves results; agents need stopping conditions, sandbox testing and guardrails.
practical_applications: Prefer fixed scripts (workflows) for repeat jobs like carousels; keep agent freedom for one-off creative judgement.
limitations: Vendor guidance dated 19 Dec 2024; page notes tooling has changed since. Author surname 'Schluntz' from prior knowledge; page showed 'Erik S.'

title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
authors: Mert Cemri; Melissa Z. Pan; Shuyi Yang; et al.
key_findings: MAST taxonomy: 14 failure modes in 3 categories from 1,642 traces of 7 MAS frameworks; human inter-annotator kappa 0.88; LLM annotator kappa 0.77.
Frequent modes: step repetition 15.7%, reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%, unaware of termination 12.4%, disobey task specification 11.8%, incorrect verification 9.1%, no/incomplete verification 8.2%.
Explicit verifiers help but are not a silver bullet - a ChatDev chess program passed superficial checks (compiles) but violated game rules.
practical_applications: Verification must test the real requirement (faceless figures, correct text), not a proxy (file exists, renders).
limitations: Coding/math tasks; percentages come from the LLM annotator.

title: AI Agents That Matter
authors: Sayash Kapoor; Benedikt Stroebl; Zachary S. Siegel; Nitya Nadgir; Arvind Narayanan
key_findings: Agent benchmarks focus too narrowly on accuracy, so state-of-the-art agents are needlessly complex and costly; jointly optimise cost and accuracy.
Weak holdouts lead to overfitting and shortcuts; non-standard evaluation practice causes widespread reproducibility problems.
practical_applications: Track cost per accepted output (quota, GPU minutes, human minutes), not only success rate.
limitations: Preprint; abstract read.

title: Who Validates the Validators? Aligning LLM-Assisted Evaluation of LLM Outputs with Human Preferences
authors: Shreya Shankar; J.D. Zamfirescu-Pereira; Bjorn Hartmann; Aditya G. Parameswaran; Ian Arawjo
key_findings: Criteria drift: users need criteria to grade outputs, but grading outputs helps them define criteria; some criteria cannot be defined before seeing outputs.
LLM-generated evaluators inherit LLM problems and need human validation; EvalGen selects evaluators that match a subset of human grades.
practical_applications: Expect the reject list (noose-like rope, faces in windows) to grow as batches are seen; update the checklist after each batch.
limitations: Qualitative user study; abstract read.

title: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter (Amazon Builders' Library)
key_findings: Retries are 'selfish'; retrying at every layer multiplies load (example: 243x on a database).
Exponential backoff with a cap plus jitter; limit retries locally with a token bucket; 'APIs with side effects aren't safe to retry unless they provide idempotency'.
practical_applications: For quota-limited APIs a retry is a spend: cap retries and never retry a daily-quota error.
limitations: High-traffic service context; page showed author first name only.

title: Site Reliability Engineering, Ch. 22: Addressing Cascading Failures
authors: Mike Ulrich; eds. Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff, Niall Richard Murphy
key_findings: Always use randomized exponential backoff; cap retries per request; use a server-wide retry budget; retry at only one layer (3 retries x 4 layers = 64 attempts).
Distinguish retriable from non-retriable errors; always set deadlines and propagate them.
practical_applications: Classify API errors: per-minute 429 = wait and retry once; per-day 429 = stop for the day.
limitations: Large-scale service context.

title: Site Reliability Engineering, Ch. 15: Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure
key_findings: A blameless postmortem records impact, mitigation, root causes and follow-up actions; triggers are defined in advance (data loss, manual intervention, a monitoring failure that led to manual discovery).
practical_applications: Studio incidents (Codex race, TTS quota burn) become short blameless postmortems in LEARNING-LOG.
limitations: Organisational practice; evidence experiential.

title: Idempotent requests (Stripe API reference)
key_findings: Idempotency keys let clients retry safely without performing the operation twice; the first result is saved and returned on retries; reuse with different parameters errors; keys pruned after >=24 h; do not use personal data as keys.
practical_applications: Name outputs by deterministic keys (kit/slide/seed) so re-running a step skips or overwrites instead of duplicating.
limitations: Payment-API specifics.

title: CWE-362: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization ('Race Condition')
key_findings: Race condition: code needs temporary exclusive access to a shared resource but a concurrent code sequence can modify it in a timing window; parent of CWE-367 (TOCTOU).
Mitigations: synchronization primitives, atomic operations, mutexes, minimise shared resources.
practical_applications: Parallel Codex runs that copy the 'newest file' from one shared folder race on a shared resource: give each run its own output path.
limitations: Security-oriented catalogue.

title: The Twelve-Factor App - III. Config
key_findings: Store config in environment variables; strict separation of config from code; litmus test: could the codebase be made open source at any moment without compromising credentials?
practical_applications: GEMINI_API_KEY stays in the user environment, never in kit files or logs.
limitations: Web-app context; author attribution from prior knowledge.

title: Secrets Management Cheat Sheet
key_findings: Avoid hardcoded secrets; detect secrets before commit (pre-commit hooks, more than one tool); rotate regularly; never log secrets - a secret in a log is exposed; avoid long-lived, broad CI credentials.
practical_applications: Add a pre-commit secret scan; scrub keys from tmp/ logs before git add.
limitations: Enterprise-oriented.

title: Docs as Code
key_findings: Documentation written with the same tools as code: issue trackers, version control, plain-text markup, code review, automated tests; teams can block merges that lack documentation.
practical_applications: SKILL.md / kit.md updated in the same commit as the script change.
limitations: Community guide; no outcome data.

title: Semantic Versioning 2.0.0
key_findings: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; once a versioned package has been released, its contents MUST NOT be modified - changes ship as a new version.
practical_applications: Never overwrite a published export; redo as v2 / 04r-1 and keep the original.
limitations: Software API context.

title: File naming conventions (Harvard Medical School Data Management)
authors: Harvard Medical School Office of Research Data Management
key_findings: Set the convention before collecting files; dates as YYYYMMDD; versions v01/v02; no spaces (use dashes/underscores); 40-50 characters; leading zeros for sequences; extra metadata in a master spreadsheet.
practical_applications: Kit folders already follow YYYY-MM-DD_NN-slug; keep slide numbers zero-padded and set numbers 3-digit-safe.
limitations: Research-data guidance.

title: C2PA Explainer, version 2.2
authors: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA)
key_findings: Content Credential (C2PA manifest) = cryptographically bound record of provenance; assertions; claim signature with X.509; hard binding (hash) and soft binding (watermark/fingerprint); durable credentials combine both.
'Provenance information alone cannot tell you whether the digital content is true, accurate or factual'; metadata can be stripped; missing credentials do not by themselves mean untrustworthy.
practical_applications: Treat provenance as disclosure, not proof of quality; expect platforms to strip or re-encode metadata.
limitations: Explainer; spec versions up to 2.5 exist.

title: IPTC NewsCodes: Digital Source Type vocabulary
key_findings: 20 terms incl. trainedAlgorithmicMedia ('Created using Generative AI'), compositeWithTrainedAlgorithmicMedia ('Edited using Generative AI', e.g., inpainting/outpainting), compositeSynthetic (composite with at least one generative AI element), digitalCapture, algorithmicallyEnhanced, minorHumanEdits.
practical_applications: Story carousel slides = trainedAlgorithmicMedia finished by code; product posts with a real cutout in an AI scene = compositeSynthetic.
limitations: Vocabulary only; embedding tools not covered.

title: Our Approach to Labeling AI-Generated Content and Manipulated Media (Meta Newsroom, with updates)
key_findings: Announced 5 Apr 2024; 'Made with AI' renamed 'AI info' on 1 Jul 2024; labels based on industry-standard AI image indicators or self-disclosure; from 12 Sep 2024 the label for content only edited with AI moved to the post menu.
practical_applications: Turn the AI label on yourself for AI-made Reels instead of relying on detection.
limitations: Policy drifts; re-check before relying. Page summary did not mention C2PA/IPTC by name.

title: PROV-Overview: An Overview of the PROV Family of Documents (W3C Working Group Note)
key_findings: Provenance = information about entities, activities and people involved in producing a piece of data or thing, usable to assess quality, reliability or trustworthiness; PROV-DM and PROV-O are W3C Recommendations dated 30 April 2013.
practical_applications: Model each kit log as entity (raw/04-2.png) - activity (flux.py, seed) - agent (FLUX schnell, human picker).
limitations: Overview only; formal definitions in PROV-DM.

title: The EU AI Act's Transparency Rules: A Practical Guide to Article 50
key_findings: Providers of generative AI must mark outputs in a machine-readable format; deployers of deepfakes must disclose; evidently artistic/fictional works may disclose in a way that does not hamper enjoyment; applies from 2 Aug 2026; systems already on the market get until 2 Dec 2026 for marking (AI Omnibus provisional agreement).
practical_applications: Direction of travel even outside the EU: label AI media and keep machine-readable marks.
limitations: Secondary guide, not the Official Journal text; Omnibus dates provisional.

title: Thailand's Advertising Guidelines Targeting AI-Generated Content
key_findings: Office of the Consumer Protection Board notification (article dated 12 Mar 2026): when AI edits make a depicted product differ from the real one, advertisers must ensure size/quantity/composition match and show clear labels such as 'Image created by AI'.
practical_applications: Product posts: the real frame stays real; AI scene labelled.
limitations: Law-firm summary; binding status not explicit on the page.

title: Automated Data Collection Terms (Meta)
key_findings: Effective 7 Oct 2024: no Automated Data Collection without Meta's express written permission; defined as collecting data from Meta products via automated or programmatic tools (scrapers, bots, spiders, crawlers).
practical_applications: Scripts that only post the user's own content are not data collection, but they automate the product UI - keep them minimal and prefer official tools.
limitations: Covers collection; posting automation falls under other terms.

title: Instagram Terms of Use (clause on unauthorized/automated access)
key_findings: Per court-filed copies and Instagram help summaries found in search: users may not create accounts or access or collect information in unauthorized ways, including automated collection without express permission.
practical_applications: Treat UI automation of Instagram as a ToS grey zone; official routes are the Meta Business Suite scheduler or the Content Publishing API.
limitations: The current official text could not be loaded (JavaScript page); wording from search results only.

title: Instagram Platform: Content Publishing
key_findings: Publishes to professional accounts: JPEG images, videos, Reels (media_type=REELS), Stories, carousels up to 20 items; limit 100 API-published posts per 24 h (another section says 50); apps that schedule must enforce the limit themselves.
practical_applications: The sanctioned alternative to browser automation for scheduling Reels.
limitations: Needs a Meta app and token; internal inconsistency on the limit.

title: Rate limits (Gemini API documentation)
key_findings: Limits on RPM, TPM and RPD; exceeding any one triggers a rate-limit error; limits apply per project, not per API key; RPD resets at midnight Pacific; tiers by cumulative spend; limits not guaranteed.
practical_applications: Midnight Pacific = 15:00 Thai time in US winter (PST), 14:00 in US summer (PDT); a second key in the same project adds no quota.
limitations: Free-tier interactive TTS limits not listed on the page; live values in AI Studio.

title: Everything you need to know about commercial print (Ghent Workgroup)
key_findings: GWG application settings in a preflight tool 'ensure problems are discovered early'; poorly configured files cause production problems, delays and unexpected costs; Ghent Output Suite helps diagnose issues.
practical_applications: Print preflight = an automated gate at handoff; same idea for exports (size, safe zone, loudness) before upload.
limitations: Trade-body page; PDF/X-4 basis from search summary.

title: Is It Worth the Time? (xkcd 1205)
key_findings: Chart of how long you can spend making a routine task more efficient before spending more time than you save over five years (e.g., 1 s saved daily ~ 30 min; 1 min saved weekly ~ 4 h).
practical_applications: Rough craft heuristic only; ignores error reduction and maintenance cost.
limitations: Webcomic, not research; year from prior knowledge.
